description: Single-panel engineering stress–strain plot (a generic XY curve plot; no sub-panels, no micrographs or insets). The x-axis is labelled "Engineering strain (%)", linear from 0 to 100 with ticks every 20; the y-axis is labelled "Engineering stress (MPa)", linear from 0 to 1200 with ticks every 200. Four colour-coded curves are identified both by inline text labels and by a colour-matched legend at lower right: black = 2Al-450°C/1h, red = 2Al-650°C/72h, green = 8Al-450°C/1h, blue = 8Al-600°C/24h. The blue curve climbs steeply to the highest stress of the group, peaking between the 1000 and 1200 MPa gridlines at roughly 38% strain, where it ends. The green curve peaks near the 900 MPa level at about 60% strain, then softens and falls to between the 600 and 800 MPa gridlines at about 72% strain. The black curve reaches between the 800 and 1000 MPa gridlines and extends furthest, to about 85% strain. The red curve lies below the black one over most of its length, crosses it near 30% strain, and terminates at about 40% strain. Both 2Al curves show a slope change with a still-positive slope around 15% strain (concave, secondary hardening stage), whereas both 8Al curves are nearly linear after yielding. The figure demonstrates that Al content and annealing state jointly control strength level, ductility and the shape (single vs. multiple hardening) of the flow curve.

observations.observation: The figure is a single engineering stress–strain plot with four colour-coded curves labelled inline and in a legend: black 2Al-450°C/1h, red 2Al-650°C/72h, green 8Al-450°C/1h, blue 8Al-600°C/24h.
Axes: x = Engineering strain (%) from 0 to 100 with gridline ticks every 20; y = Engineering stress (MPa) from 0 to 1200 with gridline ticks every 200.
The blue 8Al-600°C/24h curve attains the highest stress of the four, peaking between the 1000 and 1200 MPa gridlines at roughly 38% strain, where the curve terminates.
The red 2Al-650°C/72h curve terminates at about 40% strain, giving the shortest strain extension of the four curves, and crosses the black curve near 30% strain.
The black 2Al-450°C/1h curve extends furthest, to about 85% strain, with its plateau stress between the 800 and 1000 MPa gridlines.
The green 8Al-450°C/1h curve peaks near the 900 MPa level at about 60% strain and then softens, dropping to between the 600 and 800 MPa gridlines at about 72% strain.
Both 2Al curves (black and red) show a marked change in slope, with the slope decreasing but remaining positive, near 15% strain, whereas both 8Al curves are nearly linear after yielding.
The caption states the tests were performed at an initial strain rate of 5×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; that value is not printed anywhere on the plot itself.
The caption defines the alloys as 2Al: Fe–30.5Mn–2.1Al–1.2C (wt.%) and 8Al: Fe–30.5Mn–8.0Al–1.2C (wt.%).
The citing text states the annealing treatments are short annealing 450 °C/1 h and long annealing 2Al: 650 °C/72 h, 8Al: 600 °C/24 h, matching the inline curve labels.
The citing text reports yield stresses not printed on the figure: 2Al short annealing YS = 420 MPa, 2Al long annealing YS = 400 MPa, 8Al short annealing YS = 540 MPa, 8Al long annealing YS = 990 MPa.

The citing text reports uniform elongations for the annealed 2Al steel of UE = 75% (short annealing) versus UE = 35% (long annealing), i.e. long annealing mainly reduces uniform elongation while yield stress changes only slightly.

The citing text attributes the slope change at ~15% strain in the 2Al curves to activation of a secondary strain-hardening stage (multiple-strain-hardening behaviour) and the near-linear 8Al curves to a single hardening regime.
